analysis.one_liner: Requires tobacco companies to list cancer-causing chemicals on cigarette packages and ads, with blunt health warnings on all tobacco products.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in February 2000 and never received a hearing, a vote, or floor action before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required cigarette packages and ads to carry one of ten blunt health warnings — from "Cigarettes cause cancer" to "Smoking can kill you" — occupying a large, standardized block of every package and advertisement. It would have forced companies to print a list of the cancer-causing agents inhaled in each brand's smoke, place an insert about toxins and quitting in every pack, and report all added ingredients and nicotine, tar, and carbon monoxide yields to the government each year. It also extended strong warning labels to cigars, smokeless tobacco, and pipe tobacco, and banned advertising of all tobacco products on TV and radio.
analysis.who_benefits: People who smoke or use tobacco, and the family members who breathe their secondhand smoke, would get accurate information about what they are consuming — including a brand-by-brand list of carcinogens that companies otherwise keep private. People considering smoking, including children targeted by advertising, would face blunt warnings on every package and every ad instead of the four rotating warnings in place since 1984.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Smokers, their families, and future consumers

how_it_helps.text: Cigarette packages would have had to display one of ten plain-language warnings such as "Cigarettes cause cancer" and "Smoking can kill you," covering at least the top third of the front and back panels of every pack [S2][S3].

Every package and advertisement would have carried a statement listing the cancer-causing agents inhaled in that brand's smoke, with bold percentages showing how that brand compares to the average cigarette sold in the U.S. [S2][S3].

Tobacco manufacturers, packagers, and importers would have had to report to the government every year what ingredients they add to products and the nicotine, tar, and carbon monoxide intake from each product for average consumers, with a public toll-free number and website for the information [S2][S3].

Cigars, smokeless tobacco, and pipe tobacco — products that had little or no federally required health warning at the time — would have carried specific warnings such as "Smokeless tobacco causes mouth cancer" [S2][S3].
The bill would have let nonprofit public-health organizations go to federal court to enforce the labeling rules, with attorney's fees available if they substantially prevailed [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers, importers, and distributors would bear the cost of redesigning packages, running the mandated warnings on a third or more of every ad, compiling and disclosing ingredient and yield data, and facing civil penalties of up to $100,000 per violation per day. Retailers, billboard owners, newspapers, and magazines that sell tobacco advertising would see the value of that ad space reduced, since 30 percent or more of it would have to be a government-mandated warning.

drawbacks.text: Compliance would have fallen heavily on manufacturers and the retail and advertising businesses around them: repackaging every product, submitting marketing plans for government approval, and testing and reporting yields for each brand style, with penalties up to $100,000 per violation per day [S3].

The bill carves out trade secret and confidential business information from the ingredient disclosure, so companies could have kept some formula details from the public even under a 'right to know' law [S3].

The bill is a disclosure measure, not a restriction on sales — it informs consumers but does not itself reduce nicotine addiction or stop anyone from buying tobacco, so its public-health effect depends entirely on whether labels and warnings change behavior.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is large and one-sided in principle: tobacco is the leading preventable cause of death in the United States, and the bill would have replaced vague, decades-old warnings with blunt, brand-specific disclosure of carcinogens and addictive delivery. The costs — compliance expenses for manufacturers and lost premium value for tobacco ads — are real but modest next to the health information gained. The honest caveat is that the bill regulated information, not the product itself, and gave the industry trade-secret exemptions on its ingredients.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, and it died there when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Sen. Frank Lautenberg introduced the bill on February 29, 2000, joined by original cosponsors including Republican Sens. Richard Lugar and Lincoln Chafee and Democrat Richard Durbin [S3][S4].
Five senators cosponsored the bill, split between 2 Republicans and 3 Democrats [S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on the day it was introduced — the only action it ever received [S5].
The committee never reported the bill, held no vote, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2001, killing the bill [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers avoided mandatory blunt warnings, brand-specific carcinogen lists, and annual ingredient disclosure, and tobacco advertisers kept their ad space free of mandated warnings. Consumers gained nothing; the information the bill would have made public stayed private.

against.name: Tobacco industry
against.role: Manufacturers, importers, and advertisers of cigarettes, cigars, and smokeless tobacco
against.what_they_did: Had a direct financial stake in stopping the bill, which would have mandated blunt warnings covering a third of every package and ad, forced disclosure of added ingredients and carcinogen content, and extended broadcast ad bans to cigars and other products.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, but its sponsorship was bipartisan: a Democratic sponsor with cosponsors split 3 Democrats and 2 Republicans, so no party line can be read from a roll call.

industries.note: The bill would have forced blunt health warnings on a third or more of every package and ad, a printed list of each brand's cancer-causing agents, and annual reporting of ingredients and nicotine, tar, and carbon monoxide yields, with penalties up to $100,000 per day. Its interest lay in keeping the current four-warning regime and undisclosed formulas in place.

industries.industry: Advertising and media businesses (billboards, newspapers, magazines, broadcasters)
industries.note: Mandated warnings would have consumed at least 30 percent of every print and billboard cigarette ad and the bill would have banned all tobacco advertising on TV and radio, cutting the size and reach of a lucrative ad category. Ordinary consumers benefit from the same reduction in tobacco promotion.

Retailers and distributors would have had to carry and display the mandated warning labels and inserts and would have been liable under the bill's civil penalties. They would keep selling the products, but with more required handling and legal exposure.
